lessons.title: The Coin-Flip Game: Building Kelly From First Principles

children.text: Chapter 1 showed that a 10% bet size grew a 55%-win-rate, even-money edge faster than either 5% or 30%. That number was not chosen for convenience. It is the output of a specific calculus problem, and this lesson solves that problem from scratch, using nothing beyond probability and a derivative.

Set up the cleanest version of the problem. A bet wins with probability p and loses with probability q = 1 − p. A win pays even money: stake the same amount you could lose. You get to play this bet repeatedly, and before every round you choose what fraction f of your current capital to stake, never a fixed rupee amount. The question: which value of f grows your capital fastest over many rounds?
Why We Maximize Growth Rate, Not Expected Value
The obvious first instinct is to maximize expected profit on each individual bet. For an even-money bet, the expected return per rupee staked is straightforward:

body.latex: E[\text{return per rupee staked}] = p \cdot (+1) + q \cdot (-1) = p - q
body.caption: Positive whenever p > 0.5, and largest when the entire bankroll is staked

body.text: This framing says: since p − q is largest in absolute contribution when the stake is largest, bet everything, every time. That is obviously wrong. Stake 100% of capital on every round and the very first loss, which will eventually happen since q > 0, takes the account to zero. From zero, no future edge can ever recover anything. Maximizing expected value per bet, in isolation, ignores that bets compound: what happens on round two depends entirely on what survived round one.

children.text: Because capital compounds multiplicatively, the right quantity to optimize is not expected wealth after one bet, but the long-run growth rate of wealth across many bets. Define the growth rate over n rounds as the average log-return per round:

body.caption: By the law of large numbers, the sample fraction of wins converges to p, giving this closed form

children.text: This g(f) is exactly the function used to build Chapter 1's growth chart. Maximizing it, instead of the single-bet expected value, is the entire idea behind the Kelly Criterion.
Treat g(f) as an ordinary calculus problem. Differentiate with respect to f and set the result to zero:

body.latex: p(1-f) = q(1+f) \;\Rightarrow\; p - q = f(p+q) = f \;\Rightarrow\; f^{*} = p - q
body.caption: Since p + q = 1 by definition, the (p + q) term simply disappears

body.title: Confirm this is a maximum, not just a critical point

children.text: Setting a derivative to zero finds a critical point, which could be a maximum, a minimum, or neither. Check the second derivative:

Both terms are negative for any f strictly between −1 and 1, since p, q and every squared denominator are positive. g(f) is concave everywhere on this range, so the single critical point f* = p − q is guaranteed to be the global maximum, not a minimum or an inflection.

body.title: Solve for f*
body.prompt: Using f* = p − q, what is the optimal bet fraction for the 55%-win-rate, even-money edge from Chapter 1?
body.explanation: f* = 0.55 − 0.45 = 0.10, or 10% of capital per bet. This is precisely the fraction that grew fastest in Chapter 1's three-trader simulation. That result was not chosen by trial and error; it is the analytic solution to g'(f) = 0.

children.text: Plotting g(f) across a range of bet sizes for this same edge makes the shape of the problem visible: a peak at f* = 0.10, and a curve that turns negative well before it reaches 30%.

body.title: Growth rate g(f), p = 0.55, even-money bet

body.text: The curve crosses back to roughly zero near f = 0.20, exactly double f*. This is a general property of the even-money case: growth turns negative once you bet more than twice the optimal fraction. Chapter 1's 30% bettor was betting three times f*, deep in the territory where the same positive edge produces negative long-run growth. Chapter 5 covers this 2×f* boundary in more detail.

body.caption: Optimal fraction f* = p − q for even-money bets at different win rates

body.title: Reading the no-edge case
body.question: According to f* = p − q, what does the formula say to bet when p = 0.50 exactly?
options: 50% of capital, matching the win probability
0% of capital, since there is no edge to exploit
100% of capital, since the payoff is even money
The formula cannot be applied when p = 0.50
body.explanation: f* = p − q = 0.50 − 0.50 = 0. With no edge, the formula correctly says not to bet at all. Kelly sizing scales with edge; where there is no edge, there is no justified position, regardless of how the payoff is structured.

body.title: Verify f* by brute-force search in Python

content.caption: Grid search over f confirms the calculus result

children.text: What This Derivation Assumes, and What Comes Next

f* = p − q only holds for an even-money bet, where a win and a loss are the same size. Lesson 1.2 showed that most real trades are not even money at all. A Bank Nifty option seller's average win and average loss are rarely equal, and a trend-following swing trader deliberately seeks payoff ratios far from 1:1. The next lesson repeats this exact derivation with a general payoff ratio b, and arrives at the formula this entire course is built around.

body.text: f* = p − q is the growth-maximizing bet fraction for an even-money wager. It is the special case of the Kelly Criterion, not the whole formula, and the full version arrives in the next lesson.

points: Maximizing expected value on a single bet leads to betting everything, which guarantees eventual ruin over repeated play.
Because bets compound multiplicatively, the correct objective is the long-run growth rate, g(f) = p ln(1+f) + q ln(1-f).
Solving g'(f) = 0 gives f* = p − q for an even-money bet, and the second derivative confirms it is a true maximum.
Growth turns negative once the bet fraction exceeds roughly 2×f*, which is exactly why Chapter 1's 30% bettor lost money on a genuinely positive-expectancy edge.
This formula assumes an even-money (1:1) payoff. The next lesson generalizes it to any payoff ratio b.

body.text: f* here is the fraction that maximizes long-run growth under an idealized, repeated-bet model with known, fixed p and q. It is a mathematical target, not a recommendation to size real trades at this level. Chapter 3 explains in detail why almost no serious trader uses full Kelly in live markets. This lesson is for education only and is not investment or trading advice.
